answer: Beyond the UNSC Sanctions Lists and the lists in the Schedules to the Prevention and Suppression of Terrorism (Implementation of Security Council Resolutions) Order, 2007 already referred to [S2], a commercial bank must also verify the 'UNSCR 1718 Sanctions List of Designated Individuals and Entities' every day, taking account of any additions, deletions or other changes, and ensure compliance with the 'Implementation of Security Council Resolution on Democratic People's Republic of Korea Order, 2017', as amended from time to time by the Central Government [S4].

The RBI requires commercial banks to ensure adherence to the provisions of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 and the Rules made thereunder [S1]. Banks must also meticulously comply with any instructions or communications on the matter issued from time to time by the RBI, based on advice received from the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India [S1].
A commercial bank must review its money laundering and terrorist financing risk assessment at least annually [S1].

Under [S1], the bank must temporarily cease operations in the account until the customer submits the PAN, an equivalent e-document, or Form No. 60, and before doing so must give the customer an accessible notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard. The bank must also include in its internal policy relaxations for continued operation of accounts of customers unable to provide these documents owing to injury, illness, infirmity from old age or similar causes, subject to enhanced monitoring; if the customer instead states in writing that they do not want to submit, the bank must close the account and appropriately settle all obligations after establishing the customer's identity [S1].

A commercial bank must monitor the 'at par' cheque facility offered to co-operative banks and review such arrangements to assess the risks, including credit risk and reputational risk, arising therefrom [S4]. It must also retain the right to verify the records maintained by the customer co-operative banks/societies for compliance with the extant instructions on KYC and AML under such arrangements [S4].

For a remittance of ₹50,000 or more, a commercial bank must effect the demand draft, transfer (mail/telegraphic transfer/NEFT/IMPS or any other mode), or traveller’s cheque by debit to the customer’s account or against cheques, and not against cash payment [S1].

A commercial bank should consider the FATF Statements circulated by the RBI from time to time, along with publicly available information, for identifying countries that do not or insufficiently apply the FATF Recommendations [S1].
A commercial bank must collect an account payee cheque only for the payee constituent; it shall not collect such cheques for any person other than the payee constituent. [S1]
The commercial bank must undertake countermeasures when called upon to do so by such an international or intergovernmental organisation. [S2]

The RBI's KYC requirements operate in addition to, rather than in place of, obligations under other laws and regulations. Where applicable laws prohibit implementation of the KYC guidelines, the bank must bring this to the RBI's notice, and the RBI may advise further additional measures to manage ML/TF risks [S1]; likewise, doorstep services may be offered only after proper KYC while also complying with restrictions under Section 10(1)(b)(ii)(b) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 [S2].
Yes. A commercial bank may undertake V-CIP to carry out CDD for new customer onboarding of individual customers as well as for beneficial owners (BOs) of legal entity customers [S1].

At periodic updation of KYC, a commercial bank must obtain a self-declaration from the customer (through the registered email ID, ATMs, digital channels, a letter from an official authorised by the customer, a board resolution, etc.) where there is no change in KYC information, while ensuring that beneficial ownership information is accurate and updated as needed; where there is a change in KYC information, it must undertake a KYC process equivalent to that applicable for onboarding a new LE customer [S1]. In addition, the bank must hold KYC documents meeting current CDD standards (re-running the full onboarding-equivalent KYC process if CDD document validity has expired) and verify the customer's PAN details, if available, from the issuing authority's database at the time of periodic updation [S1].

A commercial bank must obtain any two of the specified documents (or equivalent e-documents) as proof of business/activity in the name of the proprietary firm [S1]. If the bank is satisfied that furnishing two documents is not possible, it may at its discretion accept only one, provided it undertakes contact point verification and confirms the business activity from the address of the proprietary concern [S3].
No. A commercial bank is not required to conduct customer due diligence (CDD) of all members when opening a savings bank account for an SHG; CDD of all the office bearers shall suffice [S1].
A commercial bank must categorise its customers into low, medium, and high-risk categories, based on its assessment and risk perception [S1].

A commercial bank must periodically review the risk categorisation of customer accounts at least once every six months [S1]. The bank must also establish whether enhanced due diligence measures need to be applied [S1].
A commercial bank shall disclose full-fledged information on its products and their implications to customers, so that customers can make an informed judgment about their choice of products [S1].

A commercial bank must lay down all aspects of renewal of overdue term deposits in a transparent, non-discretionary and non-discriminatory policy, and notify the customer of the renewal terms and conditions, including interest rates, at the time of acceptance of the deposit [S1]. It must obtain advance instructions for disposal of deposits on maturity in the application form and, where such instructions are not obtained, send intimation of the impending maturity date well in advance; for FCNR(B) deposits renewed within 14 days (both days inclusive) of maturity, the rate is the lower of the rates prevailing on the maturity date or the date the depositor seeks renewal, and in all other cases the overdue period is treated as a fresh term deposit [S2][S3]. Where there is no explicit mandate to renew, the bank must review such accounts to prevent them becoming unclaimed and inform the holder in writing of the inactivity and its consequences (inoperative account and fresh KYC), while for deposits frozen on law-enforcement orders it must obtain the depositor's request letter on maturity and give the depositor the option to choose the renewal term, failing which the deposit is renewed for the original term [S4][S5].

The Directions repeal the existing Directions, instructions, and guidelines relating to Responsible Business Conduct that apply to Commercial Banks, as communicated vide circular DOR.RRC.REC.302/33-01-010/2025-26 dated November 28, 2025, and anything repealed earlier remains repealed [S4]. The passages do not indicate that the Directions override or replace any other laws or regulations outside the Responsible Business Conduct framework.

You must make all printed materials used by retail customers—including account opening forms, pay-in-slips and passbooks—available in trilingual form: English, Hindi and the concerned Regional Language [S1].

A commercial bank must ensure that necessary infrastructure and facilities are put in place and appropriate security measures are taken in each branch where loans are sanctioned against gold and/or silver collateral. It must also ensure that the gold and/or silver collateral is handled only in its branches and only by its employees [S1].

A commercial bank shall be guided by the Reserve Bank's instructions on interest rates on deposit accounts and related matters as prescribed in the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 [S1]. These Directions are titled the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 [S3].

A commercial bank must pay compensation of ₹5,000 for each day of delay where it fails to adhere to the timeline prescribed in paragraph 320, i.e., processing the claim within 15 calendar days of receipt of all required documents [S1][S2].

A commercial bank should periodically organise Exporters' Meets to facilitate interaction between the bank and exporters, and these should take place at centres with a concentration of exporters [S1].

Under [S1], the policy must cover the auction procedure, including the trigger event for auction of eligible collateral and the timeline for serving an auction notice on the borrower; the mode of auction; the notice period allowed to the borrower(s)/legal heir(s) to settle the loan before auction; and the empanelment of auctioneers. It must also specify the procedure for loss, deterioration, or discrepancy in the pledged collateral (including at the time of return or auction) and the fair compensation payable to the borrower(s)/legal heir(s), with timelines [S1]. In addition, at the time of auction the bank must declare a reserve price of not less than 90 per cent of the collateral's current value, which may be reduced to not less than 85 per cent if auctions fail twice [S3].

Yes. A bank may provide additional facilities beyond the standard minimum in a BSBD account, with or without charges, provided this is done in a non-discretionary and non-discriminatory manner with transparent disclosure to the customer [S1]. The bank shall not require the customer to maintain a minimum balance in the BSBD account for such additional facilities, and their availment must be at the customer's option [S1].

The bank must undertake **at least an annual review** of accounts where there has been no customer-induced transaction for more than a year [S1]. Such reviews are required particularly for term deposits without an explicit mandate to renew, where proceeds remain unclaimed after maturity, and the bank must also notify the account/deposit holders in writing that the account would become 'inoperative' if no operations occur during the next one year [S1].

Warnings about dubious deposit schemes may be displayed or distributed in bank branches in the official language of the state, enabling easy notice by customers and helping disseminate the information to the public [S1]. The bank may also consider displaying such messages at ATMs or Business Correspondent Points, where they could get wider visibility [S1].

Yes. As the principal, the bank is responsible for the actions of its agents, including recovery agents engaged to recover its dues, and must ensure their strict adherence to the applicable instructions [S2].

The customer enquiry or "May I Help You" counter should be located near the entry point of the banking hall, and it may be either exclusively dedicated or combined with other duties [S1]. It is required at all branches, except very small branches [S1].

The prescribed post-shipment interest rate ceases from the date of credit to the banks’ ‘Nostro’ accounts [S1]. However, exporters’ credit limits remain frozen until the actual date of credit of the rupee equivalent to their account [S1].
A commercial bank must periodically undertake special drives to find out the whereabouts of customers, their nominees, or legal heirs in respect of inoperative accounts or unclaimed deposits [S1].

A commercial bank must conduct regular audits of its service providers (including subcontractors) in respect of the services outsourced to them, either through its own internal auditors or external auditors appointed on its behalf [S1]. These audits must assess the provider's performance, adequacy of its risk management practices, and compliance with laws and regulations, with frequency based on the nature and extent of risk and the impact on the bank; monitoring and control reports must be periodically reviewed by Senior Management, and any adverse development placed before the Board for information [S3]. Where multiple REs use the same third-party provider, they may adopt a pooled (shared) audit, but each RE remains responsible for ensuring that the audit requirements under its respective contract are effectively met [S2].

A commercial bank should select a group entity for outsourced services based on objective reasons similar to those used when selecting a third party, and it must appropriately deal with any conflicts of interest that the outsourcing arrangement may entail [S1].

The bank or NBFC bears responsibility for the conduct of its service provider, including Direct Sales Agents (DSAs)/Direct Marketing Agents (DMAs) and recovery agents, and must retain ultimate control over the outsourced activity [S1][S2]. The Board and senior management retain ultimate responsibility for the outsourced activity [S1][S2].

No. A commercial bank must ensure that a service provider outside the group company is not owned or controlled by any director, key managerial personnel, or approver of the outsourcing arrangement, or their relatives [S1]. However, an exception may be made with the approval of the Board or a Committee of the Board, followed by appropriate disclosure, oversight and monitoring, and the Board must ensure there is no conflict of interest when permitting such an exception [S1][S3].

Per [S1], it suffices to have clear separation and isolation of the bank's data and its customer-specific data and information, so that only personnel authorised by the bank can access data belonging to them in a multi-tenant environment or architecture.

Yes. Outsourcing arrangements shall not affect the rights of customers against the bank, including their ability to obtain redressal as applicable under relevant laws [S1][S2]. The bank must maintain a robust grievance redressal mechanism that is not compromised on account of outsourcing, and responsibility for redressing customers' grievances relating to outsourced services rests with the bank [S3][S5].

The outsourcing agreement must include the bank's right to conduct audits on the service provider, whether by its internal or external auditors or by agents appointed to act on its behalf, and to obtain copies of any audit or review reports and findings made on the service provider in conjunction with the services performed for the bank [S2]. The bank must also conduct regular audits of service providers (including subcontractors) with regard to the service outsourced by it, conducted either by internal or external auditors appointed to act on the bank's behalf [S3].

Yes. A commercial bank may outsource any IT service within its business group or conglomerate, provided the arrangement is backed by a Board-approved policy and appropriate SLAs/agreements with its group entities are in place [S1].

Yes. When multiple regulated entities use the same third-party IT service provider, they may adopt a pooled (shared) audit by pooling their audit resources or engaging an independent third-party auditor to jointly audit the common service provider, provided each entity remains responsible for ensuring that the audit requirements under its respective contract with the service provider are met effectively [S1].

When evaluating a service provider for outsourced IT services, a bank must apply the service provider evaluation requirements applicable to outsourcing of financial services (paragraphs 29–31) mutatis mutandis [S1][S3]. The additional considerations are: technology, infrastructural stability, data backup arrangements and disaster recovery plan; conflict of interest; capability to identify and segregate the bank's data; capability to comply with regulatory and legal requirements; information/cyber security risk assessment; appropriate controls, assurance requirements and contractual arrangements ensuring data protection and the bank's access to data processed, managed or stored by the provider; ability to effectively service all customers while maintaining confidentiality, especially where the provider has exposure to multiple entities; and ability to enforce agreements and the rights thereunder relating to data storage, data protection and confidentiality [S1].

A commercial bank shall create an inventory of IT services outsourced to service providers, including key entities involved in their supply chains [S2]. The bank shall also map its dependency on third parties and periodically evaluate the information received from the service providers [S2].

A commercial bank must consider the availability of alternative service providers or the possibility of bringing the outsourced activity back in-house in an emergency, along with the costs, time, and resources that would be involved [S1]. The contingency plan should also ensure business continuity, with the service provider maintaining and periodically testing robust business continuity and recovery procedures [S3][S5].

The Board, or a Committee of the Board to which powers have been delegated (as applicable for financial or IT outsourcing), is responsible for putting in place/approving the framework to evaluate the risks and materiality of all existing and prospective outsourcing arrangements [S1][S5].

Yes. The RBI outsourcing provisions apply, mutatis mutandis, to subcontracted activities, and the outsourcing contract must provide for the bank's prior approval or consent before the service provider engages any subcontractor for all or part of the outsourced activity [S3]. Before granting consent, the bank must review the subcontracting arrangement and ensure it complies with the Directions set out in Chapter III [S3].

Commercial banks shall not outsource core management functions, including Internal Audit, the compliance function, and decision-making functions such as determining compliance with KYC norms for opening deposit accounts, sanctioning loans (including retail loans), and management of the investment portfolio [S2].

A commercial bank must have in place a risk management framework that comprehensively addresses the processes and responsibilities for identification, measurement, mitigation, management, and reporting of risks associated with IT outsourcing arrangements [S1], along with a management structure to monitor and control outsourced services, covering performance, uptime of systems and resources, service availability, adherence to SLA requirements, and incident response mechanisms [S3][S4]. The IT Function must assist Senior Management in identifying, measuring, monitoring, mitigating and managing IT outsourcing risk; maintain a central database of all IT outsourcing arrangements accessible for review by the Board, Senior Management, auditors and supervisors; effectively monitor and supervise the outsourced IT service against performance standards, coordinate periodic due diligence and highlight concerns; and put in place necessary contractual documentation including service level management, monitoring of vendor operations, key risk indicators and risk-based classification of vendors [S2].
The Directions apply to commercial banks, as indicated by their title: "Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025" [S1][S2].

A commercial bank must ensure that its call centre staff are adequately trained to competently handle complaints and escalate them, if necessary [S1]. Its Grievance Redressal process must provide for automatic escalation of unresolved complaints from the call centre/base level to higher authorities, and must acknowledge complaints for follow-up through a complaint or docket number, even for complaints received over the phone [S1].
The co-branded card must explicitly indicate that the card has been issued under a co-branding arrangement [S1].

When recovering overdue dues, you and your agents must avoid actions that could damage the card issuer's integrity and reputation and must observe strict customer confidentiality [S1]. You and your agents must also adhere to the extant instructions on the Fair Practices Code for lenders, and must not indulge in mis-selling or harassment of cardholders, for which a dedicated helpline and email-id must be available to raise complaints [S2][S3]. Recovery communications must carry the name, email-id, telephone number and address of the concerned senior officer of the card-issuer, and the cardholder must be informed of the recovery agent's name and contact details immediately upon assignment [S1].

No. Prior approval of the Reserve Bank is not necessary for the issuance of co-branded debit cards, co-branded prepaid cards and co-branded credit cards, provided the conditions stipulated under the chapter are complied with [S1]. Banks also do not require prior approval to become a co-branding partner of card-issuers, and must follow the conditions set out in paragraphs 61 and 62 [S2].
The card-issuer must close the credit card account without any cost to the customer within seven working days from the date of seeking confirmation/consent from the customer [S1][S2].

For commercial banks, explicit consent is required when the credit adjustment exceeds a cut-off of one percent of the credit limit or ₹5,000, whichever is lower [S1]. If consent is not received (or no response) within seven days of the credit transaction, the card-issuer must reverse the credit transaction to the cardholder's bank account [S1].

The card-issuer must explicitly bring to the customer's notice that the information relating to the cardholder's credit history or repayment record is being provided to the Credit Information Company in terms of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005 [S1].

Every communication issued by a commercial bank's recovery agents to a credit card holder must contain the name, email-id, telephone number and address of the concerned senior officer of the card-issuer whom the customer can contact [S1].

A commercial bank may report a credit card account as 'past due' to credit information companies (CICs) or levy late payment charges only when the account remains past due for more than three days [S1][S2]. The days past due and late payment charges are computed from the payment due date mentioned in the credit card statement [S1][S2].

No. Commercial bank card-issuers shall not levy any charge that was not explicitly indicated to the cardholder at the time of issuance and without their explicit consent, except for charges like service taxes subsequently levied by the Government or any other statutory authority [S1].

Yes. Commercial banks may issue business credit cards to individuals for business expenses, as such cards are issued to business entities/individuals for business purposes and not for personal use [S1][S4].

Each card-issuer shall have a well-documented policy for the issuance and conduct of credit cards, approved by its Board or any Committee to which powers have been delegated by the Board, in consonance with RBI instructions issued from time to time and with the Directions, and available on the card-issuer's website [S1]. The policy should cover, inter alia, the interest rate ceiling and other charges, the procedure for reporting default status to a Credit Information Company (CIC), co-branding arrangements (as applicable), the standard operating procedure for discretionary blocking/deactivating/suspending a credit card, the time period for completion of formalities after blocking a lost card, and the redressal of grievances and compensation framework [S3].

A commercial bank must ensure that wrong bills are not raised and issued to cardholders. If a cardholder protests any bill, the card-issuer must provide an explanation and, wherever applicable, documentary evidence within a maximum period of 30 days from the date of complaint. [S1]

A commercial bank’s card-issuer must provide the cardholder with a term-sheet containing the Most Important Terms and Conditions (MITC), which must set out fees and charges, drawal limits, billing details (including periodicity, minimum amount payable, payment method and dispute resolution), and default and recovery procedures [S4].

Disclosure of customer information to DSAs, DMAs and recovery agents must be limited to the extent necessary to enable them to discharge their duties, and personal information provided by the cardholder that is not required for recovery purposes must not be released [S1]. The bank remains responsible for its service providers’ actions and for the confidentiality of customer information, and must ensure that these agents do not transfer or misuse customer information during marketing of credit card products [S1][S3].

A commercial bank has the freedom to determine the interest on deposits of money accepted or renewed by it under the RFC Account Scheme, in accordance with the comprehensive policy on interest rate on deposits duly approved by the Board of Directors or any Committee of the Board to which powers have been delegated [S1]. However, where an NRE term deposit is converted into an RFC account on the holder's return to India and has not run for at least one year, interest is payable at a rate not exceeding that payable on savings deposits held in RFC accounts [S2].

The bank must pay interest at the rate applicable to the amount and period for which the deposit remained with the bank, rather than at the contracted rate [S1]. No interest is payable if the premature withdrawal occurs before completion of the minimum period specified in paragraph 10(1) [S1].
The minimum tenor for NRE term deposits is one year, while the minimum tenor for NRO term deposits is seven days [S1].

A commercial bank must be authorised by the Reserve Bank of India under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) to accept rupee deposits of non-residents under NRE and NRO deposits [S1]. It must also have in place a comprehensive policy duly approved by its Board of Directors (or a Board committee to which powers have been delegated) covering interest rates on deposits and penalties for premature withdrawal of term, NRE and FCNR(B) deposits [S2].

Yes. A bank may, at its discretion, allow additional interest of one per cent per annum over and above the scheduled rate of interest on savings or term deposits to the bank's staff and their exclusive associations [S1].

When the claimant(s) of the NRE term deposit account of a deceased depositor are residents, the deposit on maturity shall be treated as a domestic rupee term deposit, with interest paid for the subsequent period at the rate applicable to a domestic term deposit of similar maturity [S1].

The interest rate on matured deposits standing in the name of a deceased individual depositor (or joint depositors where one has died) shall be as per the comprehensive policy on interest rate on deposits, subject to the conditions laid down in paragraph 7 of the Directions [S2].

The bank must bear the exchange loss arising out of the premature withdrawal if the penalty components were not clearly brought to the depositor's notice at the time of acceptance of the deposit [S1].

For an FCNR(B) deposit renewed within 14 days of maturity, the applicable rate is the appropriate interest rate for the renewal period prevailing either on the date of maturity or on the date the depositor seeks renewal, whichever is lower [S1].
Yes. Any action taken or purported to have been taken, or initiated under the repealed Directions shall continue to be governed by the provisions thereof, notwithstanding the repeal [S1].

A commercial bank is prohibited from charging a penalty for premature withdrawal of a domestic term deposit in three situations: upon the death of the depositor, even if the deposit is within the lock-in period [S1]; when the deposit amount is split at the request of the claimant(s) of a deceased depositor or joint account holders, provided the period and aggregate amount of the deposit do not undergo any change [S2]; and when depositors of a branch referred to in paragraph 7(9) desire premature withdrawal consequent to the transfer of business to another bank [S4].

Yes. A bank may, at its discretion, allow its resident Indian retired staff who are senior citizens an additional interest rate as admissible to senior citizens, over and above the additional interest payable to them by virtue of their being retired members of the bank's staff [S1].

The minimum credit balance is measured from the 10th to the last day of each calendar month, and interest, if any, on that balance shall be paid subject to the conditions in paragraph 7 of the Directions [S1].

A comprehensive policy approved by the Board of Directors (or a Committee of the Board to which powers have been delegated) must cover interest rates on deposits, penalties for premature withdrawal of term deposits including partial premature withdrawal, penalties for premature withdrawal of NRE term deposits, and penalties for premature withdrawal of FCNR(B) term deposits [S4]. Interest rates, including bulk deposit rates, must be uniform across all branches and for all customers, with no discrimination between deposits of similar amount accepted on the same date, and must strictly follow the schedule of interest rates disclosed in advance on the bank's website, with bulk deposit rates disclosed at 10:00 am (grace time of 10 minutes, latest by 10:10 am) on each business day [S4]. For NRE and FCNR(B) term deposits, the components of the penalty must also be clearly brought to the notice of depositors at the time of acceptance of the deposits [S1][S3].

Yes. Subject to the conditions in paragraph 7, a bank shall pay interest at the time of conversion of an FCNR(B) account into an RFC/Resident Rupee account even if the deposit has not completed the minimum maturity period, provided the rate does not exceed the rate payable on savings bank deposits held under the RFC Account Scheme [S1]. For a deceased FCNR(B) depositor, where the deposit is claimed before maturity, interest shall be paid at the rate applicable to the period for which the deposit remained with the bank, without charging any penalty for pre-payment [S2].

A commercial bank may extend PCFC using foreign currency funds borrowed in terms of Notification No. FEMA.3(R)/2018-RB dated December 17, 2018, as well as foreign currency funds generated through buy-sell swaps in the domestic forex market, subject to adherence to the Aggregate Gap Limit (AGL) [S3].

A commercial bank must ensure that the pre-shipment credit is liquidated out of the proceeds of bills drawn for the exported commodities, thereby converting it into post-shipment credit, and that any repayment or prepayment is made only from EEFC balances or the exporter's rupee resources to the extent exports have actually taken place [S4]. Where it extends a Pre-shipment Credit 'Running Account' facility without prior lodgement of LCs/firm export orders, the bank must judge the need for it, extend it only to exporters with a good track record (and EOUs/units in FTZs/EPZs/SEZs), and require LCs or firm orders to be produced within a reasonable period [S5].

A commercial bank's exposure by way of PCE to bonds issued by each NBFC/HFC shall be restricted to one per cent of the capital funds of the RE, within the extant single/group borrower exposure limits [S1]. Additionally, the bank's aggregate PCE exposure must not exceed 20 per cent of its Tier 1 capital [S5].

All corporates and other constituent borrowers having turnover above the threshold level fixed by the bank’s Board of Directors must disclose the ‘aging schedule’ of their overdue payables in their periodical returns submitted to banks [S1].

Under [S1], a commercial bank shall grant export credit to an exporter of good track record till the realisation of the proceeds of the cheque or draft received from abroad, after satisfying itself that the remittance is against an export order, is as per trade practices in respect of the goods in question, and is an approved method of realisation of export proceeds as per extant rules.

When introducing any new product, the bank must take into account customer suitability and appropriateness, and ensure that borrowers/customers are made fully aware of the risks and liabilities under such products [S1].

Before releasing funds, the bank must verify the genuineness of the documents to the title of the property mortgaged with it at the time of acceptance, and not defer this till the initiation of recovery proceedings. It should also obtain market reports on builders/developers and sanction loans only in respect of projects being undertaken by reputed builders/developers. [S1]

The builder/developer/company must disclose in the pamphlets/brochures the name(s) of the bank(s) to which the property is mortgaged. They must also indicate in the pamphlets/brochures that they shall provide a No Objection Certificate (NOC)/permission of the mortgagee bank for sale of flats/property, if required [S1].

Yes. A commercial bank shall not enter into lease agreements departmentally with equipment leasing companies and other NBFCs engaged in equipment leasing [S1]. This prohibition also applies to equipment leasing and hire purchase business undertaken departmentally [S2].

Bills rediscounted ‘with recourse’ in the domestic market may be reflected only in the case of the first bank discounting the bills, since that bank alone has recourse to the exporter; the bank rediscounting shall not reckon the amount as export credit [S1].

A bank should value gold or silver collateral based on the reference price corresponding to its actual purity (caratage), using the lower of (1) the average closing price for that specific purity over the preceding 30 days, or (2) the closing price for that specific purity on the preceding day, as published by the India Bullion and Jewellers Association Ltd. (IBJA) or a SEBI-regulated commodity exchange [S2]. The bank must also display on its website the methodology for determining the net weight of the gold and silver content and the price used to value it for LTV purposes [S3].

Under the RBI Directions, all collateral-free loans, irrespective of end use and mode of application, processing or disbursal (physical or digital), provided to low-income households with annual income up to ₹3,00,000 qualify as microfinance loans [S5]. To ensure the collateral-free nature, such a loan shall not be linked with a lien on the borrower's deposit account or backed by hypothecation of any security [S5].

A commercial bank must capture and maintain project-specific data in electronic and easily accessible format on an ongoing basis [S1]. The project finance database must, at a minimum, include the debtor profile (project/SPV name, PAN, LEI, sponsor names, shareholding details, banking arrangement, sector and sub-sector), the original project profile (nature of project, external credit rating, economic life, date of financial closure, original DCCO, total project cost excluding IDC, IDC, capital structure, D/E, DSCR, repayment tenor, repayment start date and repayment frequency), and details of any change in DCCO (date and reason for change, extended DCCO, revised project debt and total project cost, cost increase/overrun, percentage financed by equity and debt, and revised D/E, DSCR, repayment tenor, repayment start date, repayment frequency and external credit rating) [S1].

No. A bank shall not grant finance for construction of buildings meant purely for Government/Semi-Government offices, including Municipal offices, though it may grant loans for activities that will be refinanced by institutions like NABARD [S1].

A commercial bank may accept DLG only in one or more of the following forms: (1) cash deposited with the bank; (2) a fixed deposit maintained with a Scheduled Commercial Bank with a lien marked in favour of the bank; and (3) a bank guarantee in favour of the bank [S1].

The regulation distinguishes the two by the technology through which customers access banking services: an internet banking channel operates over the internet, including web browser-based applications but excluding mobile applications, while a mobile banking channel operates through mobile applications, USSD, and SMS [S1]. Both are digital banking channels offered for operating accounts and accessing bank services [S1].

Yes. Under paragraph 11 of the Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025, the Reserve Bank may, if it considers necessary for avoiding hardship or for any other just and sufficient reason, grant an extension of time to comply with, or exempt any regulated entity (including commercial banks) from, all or any of the provisions of these Directions, either generally or for any specified period [S1]. Any such exemption or extension is subject to such conditions as the Reserve Bank may impose [S1].

Banks must ensure continuous adherence to the provisions (as amended from time to time) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and other legal requirements, including FEMA 1999 and applicable Reserve Bank instructions, relevant DPSS instructions under the Payment and Settlement Systems (PSS) Act, 2007, and RBI instructions/Directions on KYC/AML/CFT [S1]. The jurisdiction for legal settlement is within India [S1].

Before launching, a bank must obtain prior approval from the Reserve Bank and fulfil the eligibility criteria: implementation of CBS and IPv6-enabled public-facing IT infrastructure, compliance with the minimum regulatory CRAR requirement, minimum paid-up capital/net worth as per the applicable licensing requirement as on March 31 of the immediately preceding financial year, adequate financial and technical capabilities (including the detailed report on expenditure, funds, cost-benefit analysis, technology and skilled personnel), and a satisfactory regulatory compliance track record supported by a GAICA Report certified by third-party CERT-In empaneled auditors [S1][S5]. The bank should apply to the Department of Regulation, Reserve Bank of India through the PRAVAAH portal, along with the approval of the appropriate authority and other necessary supporting documents [S1].

Yes. A commercial bank must put in place a transparent mechanism for the entire process of identifying wilful defaulters, so that penal provisions are applied in a fair manner and the scope for discretion is obviated [S1].

A commercial bank may remove a wilful defaulter's name from the List of Wilful Defaulters after entering into a compromise settlement only when the borrower has fully paid the compromise amount [S2]. A commercial bank covered under the Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS), as amended from time to time, shall comply with the directions provided under the said Scheme [S1].
